titularidad.p1: BAQUEANO is a digital platform operated and managed from Managua, Nicaragua, with reach across the entire national territory. It aims to promote sustainable tourism through technology, making it easier to connect travelers with local providers (entrepreneurs, guides, cooperatives, farms, lodgings, eateries and experiences).

naturaleza.p1: BAQUEANO is a technology platform for information, direct connection and digital facilitation. It does not provide tourism services directly; instead it offers tools so travelers can discover destinations, contact local providers and organize their experiences safely and responsibly.
naturaleza.p2: Verified tourism, cultural and natural content.
naturaleza.p3: Between travelers and local providers, without abuses.
naturaleza.p4: Routes, distances and points of interest in real time.

independencia.p1: BAQUEANO is an independent initiative and does not represent any government institution. Entities such as INTUR, MARENA, municipal governments, the National Police, Fire Department, Red Cross or other bodies are mentioned only for information purposes to guide the user. Their inclusion does not imply sponsorship, affiliation or official representation by those institutions.
independencia.strong1: BAQUEANO is not an official website of the State of Nicaragua.
independencia.p2: We are an independent platform focused on promoting sustainable and community tourism.

marcoNormativo.p1: BAQUEANO's operation is governed by the legislation in force in the Republic of Nicaragua, including:
marcoNormativo.p2: Establishes the framework for the development, regulation and promotion of tourism in Nicaragua.

gron.milestone: She shaped the country’s civic monumental memory: the Andrés Castro monument at Hacienda San Jacinto (Tipitapa), the Rubén Darío relief and the statue of the chief Diriangén.

penalba.locality: San Pedro de Lovago / San Juan de Oriente (ties to Masaya and León)
penalba.milestone: Regarded as the father of modern painting in Nicaragua and director of the National School of Fine Arts; he steered the traditional and sacred iconography of the Pacific towards the expressionist avant-garde.

morales.milestone: Born in the “Great Sultana”. His imagery projects Lake Cocibolca, colonial still lifes and the lushness of the Nicaraguan Caribbean rainforest, carried onto the international circuit (Paris, New York).

marin.milestone: Heir to the artistic tradition of the Meseta de los Pueblos; known for his visual architecture and dense palette-knife oil textures depicting Creole and urban Central American scenes.

beer.milestone: The first Afro-descendant national painter from the Caribbean Coast. Her work is living testimony to Creole identity, Black Caribbean women and the community memory of Bluefields.

arostegui.milestone: Linked to the mountainous north. Founder of the Praxis Group (1963); he introduced material informalism using soils, volcanic textures and scrap metal as a metaphor for Nicaragua’s landscape and socio-political reality.

deleon.milestone: Creator of the scraped-wax and fresco-transparency technique. He founded the Museo-Galería 904 in the capital before the 1972 earthquake, capturing the lakeside light of Managua.

saenz.milestone: The leading exponent of pictorial indigenism. He brought petroglyphs, pre-Columbian ceramics, northern legends and the line of the central highlands into contemporary murals and canvases.

saravia.milestone: A founding figure of public art in the capital and Peñalba’s right hand at the Fine Arts school; he sculpted reliefs and figures that document mestizaje and the vernacular anatomy of the Pacific.

bacon.milestone: A pioneer of Afro-Caribbean contemporary dance and Caribbean ballroom dance; she connected Maypole (Palo de Mayo) folklore and Caribbean Coast rhythms with the stages of the Pacific.

lopez.milestone: A national reference in researching and documenting marimba sones, the danzas de negras, the bailes de húngaras and the choreographic mestizaje of Monimbó and Masaya.

espinoza.milestone: Heir to León’s university intellectual tradition; her plays explore colonial memory, patriarchal oppression and the urban mythology of the country’s first capital.

montealegre.milestone: A witness through photojournalism to the insurrection, the National Literacy Crusade and post-war reconstruction; she captured everyday life in the capital’s working-class neighbourhoods.

carrion.milestone: A filmmaker who connects the collective historical memory of the 1980s with urban generational dilemmas through her documentary Heredera del viento.

pueblosOriginarios.title: Indigenous peoples of the Pacific
pueblosOriginarios.text: When the Spanish arrived, Nicaragua’s Pacific region was already home to several peoples: the Maribios or Sutiavas, the Mangues or Chorotegas, and the Nahuas or Nicaraguas. They lived in farming villages on plains near the lakes and volcanoes, were governed by councils of elders or by chiefs, and traded by barter with neighbouring peoples. Their roots are linked to migrations from the north, from lands in present-day Mexico.

conquista.title: Conquest and colonial era
conquista.text: In 1502, on his fourth voyage, Christopher Columbus sailed along Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast and rounded a cape he named Gracias a Dios. In 1522, Gil González Dávila and Andrés Niño arrived overland from Panama and made contact with the chiefs Nicoya and Nicaragua. In 1524 the Spanish founded León and Granada, and in 1544 the territory became part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala.

leonViejo.title: León Viejo
leonViejo.text: León, one of the cities founded by the Spanish in 1524, was moved to its current site in 1610 after an earthquake. The ruins of the original city, known as León Viejo, were added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2000.

independencia.title: Independence
independencia.text: The first independence uprisings broke out in 1811 in León, Granada and Rivas, with strong popular support. The Captaincy General of Guatemala, which included Nicaragua, declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821. A year later it was annexed to Agustín de Iturbide’s short-lived Mexican Empire, and in 1823 Nicaragua joined the Federation of the United Provinces of Central America.

treintaAnos.title: The Thirty Years
treintaAnos.text: After William Walker’s filibuster incursion, the Nicaraguan State slowly took shape. This period is known as the Thirty Years: it runs from the administrations of General Tomás Martínez, between 1858 and 1867, to 1893, the year of the liberal revolution.

guerraNacional.title: National War
guerraNacional.text: Between 1855 and 1857, Nicaragua faced the filibuster incursion of William Walker. In the north, Generals Tomás Martínez and Fernando Chamorro organised the Army of the North (Ejército del Septentrión), whose officers declared in Matagalpa on 20 April 1856 that they would defend national independence to the last drop of blood. Six months of that resistance led to the Battle of San Jacinto.

sanJacinto.title: The Battle of San Jacinto
sanJacinto.text: On Sunday, 14 September 1856, at the San Jacinto hacienda, Colonel José Dolores Estrada and his troops held off the filibusters’ attack. The fighting was hand to hand, and Andrés Castro, with no time to load his rifle, brought down a filibuster with a stone. A flanking sortie surprised the attackers, who fled. That same day, Estrada reported the victory in his official dispatch.

dario.title: Rubén Darío
dario.text: Félix Rubén García Sarmiento was born in Metapa on 18 January 1867 and died in León on 6 February 1916. His father’s family was known as the Daríos, which is why he took the surname Darío. A poet, journalist and diplomat, he is regarded as the foremost representative of literary modernism in the Spanish language.

sandino.title: Augusto C. Sandino
sandino.text: Augusto Nicolás Calderón Sandino was born in Niquinohomo, Masaya, on 18 May 1895. In 1927 he began the armed struggle against the United States intervention at the head of the Army in Defence of National Sovereignty. He was assassinated on 21 February 1934 by National Guard officers acting on the orders of Anastasio Somoza García.

costaCaribe.title: The Caribbean Coast and the Mosquitia
costaCaribe.text: The history of Nicaragua’s Caribbean followed its own path. In the 18th century the English allied with the Miskito people and consolidated their hold on the region; in 1748 they seized San Juan de Nicaragua. The Mosquitia, or Mosquito Coast, came to be regarded as an English colony until 1860, when the Treaty of Managua recognised Nicaragua’s sovereignty and created the Mosquitia Reserve.

autonomia.title: Autonomy of the Caribbean Coast
autonomia.text: In 1987 Law No. 28, the Statute of Autonomy of the Regions of Nicaragua’s Caribbean Coast, was approved. The law symbolised the recognition of the ancestral rights of Indigenous and Afro-descendant peoples as the country’s multi-ethnic, multicultural and multilingual communities.

patrimonioMundial.title: Nicaragua’s World Heritage
patrimonioMundial.text: Nicaragua has two properties on UNESCO’s World Heritage List: the Ruins of León Viejo, inscribed in 2000, and León Cathedral, inscribed in 2011.

gueguense.title: El Güegüense
gueguense.text: El Güegüense is a satirical drama, well known in Nicaragua, that brings together theatre, dance and music as a synthesis of Spanish and Indigenous cultures. It is performed every year at the feast of San Sebastián. UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005 and inscribed it in 2008 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

legalFrameworkSection.p1: Tourism development in Nicaragua rests on the current legal framework promoted by INTUR and the National Assembly, guaranteeing tax incentives for local businesses and recognizing 13 official categories of tourism activity.
legalFrameworkSection.p2: It sets the guiding principles of sustainability, competitiveness and sovereignty of Nicaraguan tourism. Article 16 defines and classifies the official tourism categories that energize territories and promote community inclusion.

faqList.div1: Does Baqueano charge any commission on my sales?
faqList.div2: No. The Baqueano model is designed to eliminate financial intermediation. The explorer pays your cooperative or business directly. Baqueano facilitates the connection but does not touch or retain any percentage of your income. This is what we call "tourism with rural sovereignty".
faqList.div3: Do I need INTUR registration to join?
faqList.div4: It is not a strict requirement to sign up, but it is highly recommended. INTUR registration gives you access to the incentive regime of Laws No. 1210 and 1211, which promote community tourism development. The Baqueano team can guide you through INTUR registration if you need it.
faqList.div5: How long until my business appears in the app?
faqList.div6: Once your request is sent, the General Administrator reviews it in the Ops Center within 48-72 business hours. If the information is correct and verifiable, your business is published on the web map and in the Android app. You'll receive a confirmation email with your official host badge.
faqList.div7: What is the trail GPS beacon system?
faqList.div8: GPS beacons are satellite safety points that baqueano guides activate in the Android app when starting a tour. Explorers and their emergency contacts can see the location in real time. If an incident occurs, the SOS feature sends exact coordinates to emergency numbers and to the Baqueano Desk's WhatsApp.
faqList.div9: How do I receive payments from explorers?
faqList.div10: Payment is 100% direct: the explorer coordinates with you by WhatsApp, email or phone, and pays however you both prefer (cash, transfer, bank deposit). Baqueano shows your direct contact on your profile. There is no intermediary payment gateway. Integration with Tilopay/BAC will soon be available for those who want it, but always optional and without Baqueano commissions.
faqList.div11: Can I update my business information later?
faqList.div12: Yes. Once your registration is approved, you'll get access to a management portal where you can update prices, schedules, photos and availability. Changes go through a quick review by the Administrator (usually less than 24 hours) before appearing in the app and on the website.

sec1.div2: (website, Android application and related digital services), operated to promote sustainable tourism, living culture, nature and the strengthening of local communities in Nicaragua. By entering, browsing or interacting with our channels, the user declares having read, understood and accepted all of these provisions.

sec2.p1: Key concepts used on the platform.
sec2.div1: For the purposes of these terms:
sec2.div2: refers to the technological and institutional solution;
sec2.div3: refers to any person who browses or books;
sec2.div4: includes accredited guides, local baqueanos, community cooperatives and tourism entrepreneurs;
sec2.div5: refers to the artificial intelligence and territorial recommendation models.

sec3.div1: Access to and use of the services constitutes express acceptance of these Terms and our Privacy Policy. Anyone who disagrees with any section must refrain from using the platform. Any update published at this same URL takes effect immediately.

sec4.p1: Terms of use, scope of services and restrictions.
sec4.div1: The platform is intended exclusively for information, planning and community connection purposes. Any unlawful use, massive automated data extraction (unauthorized scraping) and any conduct that violates the territorial or environmental sovereignty of Nicaragua's nature reserves are prohibited.

sec5.p1: Creating credentials, security and user responsibility.
sec5.div1: To access features such as favorites, itinerary history in My Trip or environmental alert reports, users can register by email or federated authentication (Firebase Auth). Each user is responsible for keeping their password confidential.

sec6.p1: Profile information, privacy and accuracy of the data provided.
sec6.div1: Users agree to enter truthful information and keep it up to date. BAQUEANO reserves the right to remove fictitious profiles or those used for impersonation.

sec7.p1: The role of local entrepreneurs, cooperatives, guides and businesses.
sec7.div1: Local providers operate autonomously. BAQUEANO acts as a bridge for visibility and technological facilitation, without oppressive intermediation or extractive commissions on their community livelihood base rates.

sec8.p1: Geographic, climate, cultural and conservation data.
sec8.div1: The profiles of Nicaragua's 29 destinations and reserves are compiled from institutional sources (INTUR, MARENA) and direct testimony from local guides. Although they are updated periodically, climate or physical access conditions on site may vary.

sec9.p1: Terms for direct booking and payment at the destination or via partner gateways.
sec9.div1: Payments go directly to the local provider or through verified payment links agreed with cooperatives. BAQUEANO does not hold hosts' funds or charge hidden fees to explorers.

sec10.p1: Cancellation policies according to the type of experience and weather conditions.
sec10.div1: Each cooperative and host sets its own notice periods for penalty-free cancellation. In situations of official environmental or weather alerts, rescheduling or a full refund takes priority.

sec11.p1: Transparency in national currency (Córdoba Oro C$) with USD reference.
sec11.div1: Official prices are expressed in córdobas (C$) with US dollars as a reference. There are no surprise service charges at the end of the booking.

sec12.div1: The "BAQUEANO Verified" badge certifies that our team or the community has audited in person the provider's ownership, GPS coordinates, direct contact, real photos and hospitality practices.

sec13.p1: Scope of the travel assistant, algorithms and disclaimer.
sec13.div1: Baqueano Digital uses generative AI models to structure routes and itineraries. Its suggestions are guidance only and should be checked with local hosts and on-site conditions before setting out.

sec14.p1: Satellite accuracy, GPS use and offline maps.
sec14.div1: The platform's maps rely on satellite data and open-source cartography. In rugged areas or volcanic craters, the GPS signal may be affected by terrain and vegetation.

sec15.p1: Reviews, photos, ratings and citizen alerts.
sec15.div1: Comments provided by travelers must be truthful and respectful. Defamatory content, hate speech or material that encourages environmental harm to wild flora and fauna will not be tolerated.

sec16.p1: Rules of ethical behavior in rural and indigenous communities.
sec16.div1: Travelers agree to respect local rules of coexistence, ask permission before photographing residents or ancestral ceremonies, and follow the instructions of the accompanying baqueano or guide.

sec17.p1: Rights over the BAQUEANO brand, code, design and iconography.
sec17.div1: All logos, designs, source code, illustrations of the Guardabarranco Baqüi and editorial texts are the exclusive property of BAQUEANO or are used under legitimate licenses.

sec18.p1: Real photographs of the territory and copyright.
sec18.div1: The photographs shown are of landscapes, producers and partners in Nicaragua. Their external commercial reproduction without prior written consent is prohibited.

sec19.p1: Links to external services, WhatsApp and official sites.
sec19.div1: The platform may include links to WhatsApp for direct contact or to government institutions. BAQUEANO does not control the privacy policies or operation of those external services.

sec20.p1: Exclusion of indirect damages and risks inherent to ecotourism.
sec20.div1: Ecotourism and mountaineering involve natural risks (weather, steep trails, wildlife). Travelers knowingly take responsibility for their own physical safety and agree to hire properly accredited guides.

sec21.p1: Service "as is" and continuous server availability.
sec21.div1: We work with high-availability cloud infrastructure, but we do not guarantee uninterrupted service in areas without mobile coverage or during scheduled maintenance.

sec22.p1: Green Decalogue, leave-no-trace principles and ecological respect.
sec22.div1: All users agree not to remove geological samples or protected fauna or flora, to take their own trash back with them and to respect marked trails in biosphere reserves and national parks.

sec23.p1: 24/7 SOS button protocol and coordination with authorities.
sec23.div1: The SOS feature is a digital channel for liaison and guidance with pre-calculated GPS coordinates. It does not replace emergency rescue services or the public security forces of the State of Nicaragua.

sec24.p1: Disciplinary measures for serious misconduct or fraud.
sec24.div1: BAQUEANO may immediately suspend or disable accounts involved in financial fraud, identity theft or flagrant disregard of environmental conservation rules.

sec25.p1: Technical evolution and progressive improvements to the platform.
sec25.div1: We reserve the right to add new tools, optimize mapping algorithms or remove obsolete features for the benefit of the traveler experience.

sec26.p1: Notification of substantial changes to the community.
sec26.div1: Any substantive change will be duly communicated, with the date of the last update shown at the top of this page.

sec27.p1: Legal framework of the Republic of Nicaragua.
sec27.div1: These terms are governed by and interpreted in accordance with the laws in force in the Republic of Nicaragua. For any legal dispute, the parties submit to the jurisdiction of the courts of the city of Managua.

sec28.p1: Prior stage of friendly dialogue and community mediation.
sec28.div1: In the event of any disagreement, the parties agree to first go through a stage of friendly dialogue and direct mediation with the participation of local guide committees and the BAQUEANO team.
